subtype: Approach: rehearsing in front of a mirror or family [Action]
passage:
After dinner, Jomon stood on the living room carpet with a folded paper. Neelam didi sat on the sofa, Mummy at the table, Papa with his tea.
Jomon: My poem is called 'Rain on the Roof'. Ready? Rain-on-the-roof-rat-a-tat...
Neelam: Slow down! We can't catch a word.
Jomon: Sorry. Rain on the roof, rat-a-tat-tat...
Papa: Look up from the paper, Jomon. Look at us.
Mummy: And pause after each verse.
Jomon tried again, slower, eyes up. Neelam clapped. "Now I can hear the rain," she said. He practised twice more, and on the day of the recital he did not rush at all.

qa.q: What is the name of Jomon's poem?
qa.a: The poem is called 'Rain on the Roof'.

qa.q: What might Jomon be feeling as the family listens and gives advice?
qa.a: Jomon is probably nervous but willing, since he tries again after each tip and grows steadier.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Jomon use to prepare, and why?
qa.a: Jomon could record himself reciting or practise in front of a mirror. Hearing or seeing himself shows where he rushes or looks down.

qa.q: How does Neelam see Jomon's poem after the tips?
qa.a: Neelam said 'Now I can hear the rain', so Neelam finds the slower version clearer and enjoys it more.

grounding: A boy practises his poem in front of his family after dinner, they tell him to slow down and look up, and he improves before the day.

subtype: Approach: imagining the stage and how he will walk in [Thinking]
passage:
Backstage, Rashmi Ma'am found Rishabh standing with his eyes shut in the wings.
Rashmi: Are you all right?
Rishabh: I'm walking, ma'am. Out of the curtain, ten steps to the red spot, stop, feet together.
Rashmi: And then?
Rishabh: I look at the back row, take one breath and say the first line. In my head, it's already happened.
Rashmi: Why do it in your head?
Rishabh: Because when it's the real one, I won't be surprised by anything. I've been there before.
Irawati whispered from the curtain, "Two minutes!" Rishabh opened his eyes and nodded.

qa.q: How many steps does Rishabh count to the red spot?
qa.a: Rishabh counts ten steps to the red spot.

qa.q: What does Rishabh feel about the real moment because of his picture in his head?
qa.a: Rishabh feels calmer and readier, since picturing each step means the real moment holds fewer surprises.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Rishabh use, and why?
qa.a: Rishabh could walk the real stage once before the show or rehearse with friends watching. Being on the real spot gives even more certainty than imagining.

qa.q: How might Irawati see Rishabh's imagining?
qa.a: Irawati whispered that two minutes remained, so Irawati may see Rishabh as calm and ready, and be reassured by that.

grounding: A child closes his eyes and pictures walking on to the stage, standing at the spot and beginning, so the real moment feels less surprising.

subtype: Approach: practising only the parts she already knows well [Pitfall]
passage:
At home, the night before the school concert:
Rashmi: Trisha, sing me the whole song.
Trisha: Okay. Golden fields, silver rain... (she sings the first verse beautifully).
Rashmi: Now the second verse.
Trisha: Later, Amma. Let me do the first one again. I like it best.
The next day, backstage:
Trisha: I nailed the first verse! But then... Amma, the second verse just went. My mind was blank. I hummed and stood there.
Rashmi: I saw. Everyone heard the pause.
Trisha: I only practised the part I liked. The rest I barely touched.

qa.q: Which verse did Trisha keep practising at home?
qa.a: Trisha kept practising the first verse.

qa.q: What might Trisha feel backstage after forgetting the second verse?
qa.a: Trisha probably feels embarrassed and disappointed, since the blank and the humming happened in front of everyone. 😔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Trisha use next time, and why?
qa.a: Trisha could give the hardest or least known parts the most practice, or sing the whole song from the start each time. That way every verse is ready on the stage.

qa.q: How might Rashmi see the concert moment?
qa.a: Rashmi saw and heard the pause, and answers gently, so Rashmi probably feels sympathetic and wants Trisha to learn from it without being blamed.

grounding: A girl keeps repeating the first verse she enjoys, and on stage she forgets the second verse she has barely practised.

subtype: Approach: worrying so much that he stops practising [Pitfall]
passage:
Aadhya: Pradeep, you haven't practised your part today.
Pradeep: I can't, Didi. Every time I start, I see everyone laughing.
Aadhya: Nobody is going to laugh.
Pradeep: What if they do? My stomach hurts just thinking about it.
Aadhya: The show is in three days. You've done it twice all week.
Pradeep: I know! That's why I feel worse. I haven't practised, so I'll mess up, so I'm scared, so I don't practise.
Aadhya: That's going round in circles, Pradeep.
Pradeep: I know. But I still can't open the script.
He sat on the bed, the script closed beside him.

qa.q: How many days were left until the show?
qa.a: Three days were left until the show.

qa.q: What is Pradeep afraid of, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Pradeep is afraid that everyone will laugh, and the stomach ache and avoiding the script show how strong the fear is. 😰

qa.q: What alternative approach could Pradeep try, and why?
qa.a: Pradeep could practise just one line aloud with Aadhya listening, then add another. A tiny step is easier to begin than the whole script and can break the cycle.

qa.q: How does Aadhya see Pradeep's worry?
qa.a: Aadhya points out that the cycle goes round in circles and reminds Pradeep of the three days left, so Aadhya seems worried and wants to help.

grounding: A boy imagines everyone laughing and feels sick, so he avoids rehearsing, and with less practice he becomes more nervous in a worry cycle.

subtype: Approach: calming with slow breaths before going on [Action]
passage: The curtain was two minutes from opening. Vasudha stood in the wings in her yellow costume, and her heart beat so hard she could feel it in her ears. Charu, next to her, was fidgeting with a bangle. "Do the breathing," whispered Vasudha, remembering what the dance teacher had shown the group. She breathed in through her nose, counting one, two, three, four. Then out through her mouth, one, two, three, four. Again. Again. Her hands stopped shaking. Her heartbeat slowed, and her shoulders dropped. When the music began she stepped forward, not calm exactly, but steady enough to start.

qa.q: What colour was Vasudha's costume?
qa.a: Vasudha's costume was yellow.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling before the curtain opened?
qa.a: Vasudha was nervous, shown by her loud heartbeat and shaking hands, until the slow breaths steadied her.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Vasudha use if breathing is not enough, and why?
qa.a: Vasudha could tell the first step of the dance to herself or hold a friend's hand for a moment. A small thing to focus on gives the mind somewhere to go.

qa.q: How might Charu see Vasudha's breathing?
qa.a: Charu was fidgeting with a bangle and heard the whisper to breathe, so Charu may find it a comfort and may copy it to settle down too.

grounding: Before the dance a girl breathes in slowly for four counts and out for four, as her teacher showed the group, so her heart slows and her hands steady.

subtype: Approach: planning what to do if she forgets a line [Thinking]
passage: I'm Omkar, and I was in the audience during rehearsal when Parveen stopped mid-scene, looking worried. She turned to the teacher afterwards. "What if I forget my line on the day?" The teacher did not say 'you won't'. Instead they sat on the stage steps and made a plan together. If Parveen forgets, she pauses, takes a slow breath, and looks at Tara, who says the next line. Parveen repeated it twice, then practised it, even pretending to forget a line so she could try the pause. During the show she did forget, once, and it worked: the pause was so short that most people never noticed.

qa.q: Who says the next line if Parveen forgets?
qa.a: Tara says the next line.

qa.q: What was Parveen worried about after the rehearsal?
qa.a: Parveen worried about forgetting her line on the day, and wanted a plan for it.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Parveen use as well, and why?
qa.a: Parveen could keep a small cue word in mind or practise the line with friends until it is automatic. More than one safety net gives even more calm.

qa.q: How does Omkar see the plan?
qa.a: Omkar watched from the audience and saw the pause work, so Omkar probably feels impressed by how a small plan kept the show moving.

grounding: A girl asks what if she forgets and plans with her teacher to pause, breathe and look at Tara who has the next line, seen by an observer.

subtype: Approach: recording a practice and noticing mistakes [Revision]
passage: Note from Suraj's mother, evening. Suraj asked to borrow my phone and took it to his room. When I looked in, he was recording his speech for the school assembly, then playing it back with a frown. "I sound like a train," he said. "And I mumble the last words." He wrote 'pause' in the margin after every sentence and tried again. His little brother Mohit giggled outside the door, but Suraj ignored him. He recorded it a second time and listened. "Better," he said, "I can hear every word." He seemed relieved, and asked for the phone again in the morning.

qa.q: What did Suraj write in the margin after every sentence?
qa.a: Suraj wrote 'pause' in the margin after every sentence.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel after listening to the second recording?
qa.a: Suraj was relieved and satisfied, since every word could be heard and he asked for the phone again in the morning.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Suraj use to improve, and why?
qa.a: Suraj could practise in front of a small audience or ask a family member to signal when he speeds up. Live feedback adds to what a recording shows.

qa.q: How might Mohit see Suraj's practice?
qa.a: Mohit giggled outside the door and was ignored, so Mohit may see it as funny, or may feel left out of the serious work.

grounding: A boy records his speech on his mother's phone, notices he speaks too fast and mumbles the end, then pauses after each sentence and re-records to compare.

subtype: Approach: continuing smoothly after a mistake on stage [Revision]
passage: In the school hall in Toronto, the music swelled and Yael took her place for the group dance. Halfway through, her feet went left when everyone else went right. For one heartbeat the hall seemed to hold its breath. Yael smiled, listened for the drum, and slipped into the next move with the others as if it had been planned. Bilal, next to her, grinned. By the final pose, she was in step. Afterwards a parent told the teacher how beautiful it was, and Yael's mistake was never mentioned. Yael felt her face go warm, but it was from happiness now.

qa.q: Where did the dance take place?
qa.a: The dance took place in the school hall in Toronto.

qa.q: What did Yael feel after the dance?
qa.a: Yael felt relieved and happy, shown by the warm face and the fact that the slip went unnoticed. 😊

qa.q: What alternative approach could Yael use if she loses her place again, and why?
qa.a: Yael could watch a friend such as Bilal and follow the next move. Following a neighbour gets back into the flow quickly.

qa.q: How might Bilal see Yael's slip?
qa.a: Bilal grinned next to Yael, so Bilal probably saw a dancer recover gracefully and felt proud, not embarrassed on Yael's behalf.

grounding: During the show a girl mixes up a dance step, smiles, picks up the beat and joins the next move, so most of the audience never notices.

subtype: Approach: finding out the topics and format first [Thinking]
passage: In the small town's government school, the headmaster pinned a notice on the board: inter-school quiz, next month. Sunil read it twice. Then, instead of rushing off to memorise everything, he asked Gargi Ma'am, "What subjects will it cover, and how are the rounds?" She checked the circular. "Science, sports and general knowledge, and there are buzzer rounds." Sunil sat down with a pencil. "So fast recall matters, and I should read about all three. Not history or maths so much." He listed sports records first, then science facts, and decided to practise answering aloud quickly, as if a buzzer had sounded.

qa.q: Which subjects would the quiz cover?
qa.a: The quiz would cover science, sports and general knowledge.

qa.q: How does Sunil feel about the quiz once he knows about the buzzer rounds?
qa.a: Sunil feels focused and determined; he plans to practise answering aloud quickly, as if a buzzer had sounded, because fast recall matters.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Sunil use to prepare, and why?
qa.a: Sunil could join a partner for practice rounds or read widely from newspapers. Practice with another person shows how quickly he actually answers.

qa.q: How does Gargi Ma'am help Sunil?
qa.a: Gargi Ma'am checked the circular and gave the details, so the teacher helps Sunil aim his study at the right topics.

grounding: A boy learns the quiz covers general knowledge, science and sports with buzzer rounds, so knowing the format tells him what to prepare and how quickly to answer.

subtype: Approach: reading widely from newspapers and books [Action]
passage: Sunday night. Diary, my quiz plan is going well. Every day at breakfast I read the newspaper's page for children, and at night I read a chapter of my general knowledge book. Each time I find something new, I write it in a small blue notebook: places, people, records. Today I wrote that the tallest waterfall is in South America, and that a famous marathon runner comes from Kenya. It's fun, like collecting stamps. Mehak tested me at lunch and I got seven right out of ten. I want to read the sports page too tomorrow. Vidya.

qa.q: Where does Vidya write new facts?
qa.a: Vidya writes new facts in a small blue notebook.

qa.q: Why does Vidya say the reading feels like collecting stamps?
qa.a: Vidya finds each new fact enjoyable and worth keeping, which shows a happy and curious mood.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Vidya add, and why?
qa.a: Vidya could practise with a partner using mock rounds. Reading adds facts, but answering questions aloud shows what has really stuck.

qa.q: How might Mehak see Vidya's preparation?
qa.a: Mehak tested Vidya at lunch and saw seven out of ten right, so Mehak probably sees steady progress and may feel encouraged too.

grounding: A girl reads the newspaper's page for children each day and a general knowledge book at night, and keeps a notebook of new facts.
